claims.text: The proposed material system is CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy-alloy multilayers.
Reducing interface coherency by introducing lattice mismatch will cause a transition from diffusion-mediated creep to dislocation-mediated creep.
The initial CoCrFeMnNi multilayers have fully coherent interfaces.
Diffusion-dependent creep dominates in the coherent-interface multilayers at high temperature.
Controlled lattice mismatch can transform fully coherent multilayer interfaces into semi-coherent interfaces.
The coherency-to-semi-coherency transformation generates misfit dislocations at the interfaces.
Temperature and stress regimes exist in which both diffusion creep and dislocation creep can occur in these multilayers.
The degree of interface coherency can be characterized by the density of misfit dislocations at multilayer boundaries.
Fully coherent interfaces facilitate atomic diffusion along the interface.
Enhanced atomic diffusion along coherent interfaces favors diffusion-mediated creep.
Lattice mismatch and associated interfacial defects create local barriers affecting dislocation motion.
Local stress fields and barriers associated with misfit dislocations promote dislocation slip.
Semi-coherent interfaces shift the dominant creep mechanism toward dislocation-mediated behavior.
Semi-coherent-interface multilayers will exhibit increased dislocation activity.
Semi-coherent-interface multilayers will have a lower contribution from diffusion-controlled creep.
Changing interface coherency will produce measurable changes in creep rates and creep curves.
The mechanism transition is sensitive to the amount of lattice mismatch and to temperature and stress.
Outside specific temperature and stress ranges, reducing interface coherency may not substantially change the dominant creep mechanism.
The threshold lattice mismatch required for the proposed mechanism transition is unknown.
The quantitative change in creep rate cannot be specified without systematic experimental calibration.
